title: Carciofi alla Romana
subtitle: Artichokes braised in olive oil with mint and garlic
excerpt: Carciofi alla romana are whole globe artichokes stuffed with mint, parsley, and garlic, then braised upside down in a shallow pool of olive oil and water until completely tender. They are one of the defining vegetable dishes of Roman Jewish cooking and are at their best in spring when the violet artichokes of Lazio are in season.
sourceNotes: Carciofi alla romana is a staple of Roman Jewish cooking and one of Rome's most celebrated vegetable dishes. It is traditionally made with the mammole or romanesco artichoke variety, which has no choke, and is documented throughout Roman cookery literature.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook up to 2 hours ahead and serve at room temperature.

content.text: Carciofi alla romana requires trimming the artichokes to remove the tough outer leaves and expose the heart, then opening the leaves enough to stuff them with a simple filling of mint, parsley, and garlic. They cook upside down, stems pointing upward, so the olive oil and water steam the artichokes from below while the stems also cook through. The dish is vegan and utterly simple once the preparation is mastered.

Fill a large bowl with water and the juice of {{lemon}} lemon. Working with each artichoke in turn, snap off the tough outer leaves until you reach the pale, tender inner leaves. Trim the base flat and peel the stem with a peeler. Cut the top third off the artichoke. Open up the centre leaves with your fingers and use a small spoon to scrape out any fuzzy choke if present. Drop into the acidulated water.

Mix together {{mint}} of mint, {{parsley-flat}} of parsley, {{garlic}} of grated garlic, a pinch of {{salt-table}} salt, and a drizzle of oil. Drain the artichokes and stuff a little of the herb mixture into the centre of each one, pressing between the leaves.

Choose a saucepan that fits the {{globe-artichoke}} artichokes snugly when placed upside down (stems pointing up). Pour in {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of olive oil and 150 ml of water. Stand the artichokes upside down in the pan -- they should be packed closely so they hold each other upright. Drizzle a little more oil over the stems and season.

Bring to a simmer over a medium heat, then cover and reduce to low. Cook for 35 to 40 minutes until the artichokes are completely tender when a knife is inserted into the base. The liquid should be mostly absorbed. Serve warm or at room temperature with any remaining cooking oil drizzled over.

items.symptom: The artichokes are still tough after 40 minutes
items.cause: The artichokes were large or not fully trimmed, or the heat was too low.
items.fix: Add a splash more water and continue cooking, covered. Artichoke cooking time varies with size. The base must be completely soft when probed.

content.text: Carciofi alla romana is the braised counterpart to carciofi alla giudia (the fried version). Both dishes are central to Roman Jewish cooking, which developed many of the most celebrated vegetable preparations in Italian cuisine. The braised version is gentler and more fragrant: the mint in the stuffing is the key flavour, and it permeates the artichoke as it cooks. The dish is eaten as an antipasto, a side dish, or sometimes as a first course on its own.
